newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court sides with Honda on seatbelt ruling.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court sides with Honda on seatbelt ruling.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday let stand a ruling that federal motor vehicle safety standards shield automakers from state liability lawsuits in a case involving Honda Motor Co. Ltd.

The justices declined to review a ruling by a U.S. Court of Appeals based in Denver for Honda in a product liability lawsuit alleging the carmaker defectively designed the seatbelt used in the 1988 Honda Prelude.

The appeals court also held that the plaintiff who filed the lawsuit could not present evidence that Honda could have used an alternative system containing, in part, an airbag. It said federal motor safety rules preclude such evidence.

The case stemmed from a 1990 accident in which Diane Montag drove onto a railroad crossing in Westminter, Colorado. A freight train hit her car and she was thrown from the vehicle, despite wearing a seatbelt.

The crash had forced the car door open, and since the safety belt was attached to the door it released her. Montag later died from her injuries, and a lawsuit filed by her husband charged Honda with negligence and defective design of the seatbelt.
But a jury and then the appeals court ruled for Honda, finding that the door-mounted safety belt was not defectively designed because it met federal motor vehicle safety standards.
Attorneys representing Montag urged the Supreme Court to hear the case, but the justices sided with Honda and denied the appeal without comment or dissent.
